newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi sells most of its coffee despite sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Burundi sells most of its coffee despite sanctions.

text.p: Burundi has sold 92 percent of its 1996/97 coffee crop, its main foreign exchange earner, despite civil war and economic sanctions, coffee officials said.

A total of 25,000 tonnes of mild arabicas were produced in 1996/97 and 23,000 tonnes had already been sold, Thomas Minani, general manager of the state-owned Burundi Coffee Office (OCIBU), said on Tuesday. Much of the crop had been exported by air.
"We have sold about 23,000 tonnes so far," Minani said.
The rest would be sold at a series of auctions before the end of August with 500 tonnes on sale on Wednesday, he added.
Production in 1997/98 would fall to a little over 20,000 tonnes because of a long dry season from December to January.
But quality was good, with 70 percent of production higher quality fully washed courant and the rest washed, Minani said.
Burundi would normally produce about 30,000 tonnes, but an ethnic civil war in which more than 150,000 people have died since October 1993 has reduced production.

"The quality of last year's (1996/97) crop is of average or medium quality because farmers were not able to take care of their fields. It is because of the war. If farmers are in refugee camps they cannot take care of their fields," coffee exporter Euphrasie Mashwabure told Reuters.

But Mashwabure and other traders said the civil war's impact on coffee paled by comparison with the difficulties that followed the imposition of regional sanctions last July after a coup brought military leader Pierre Buyoya to power.
Sanctions cut off supplies of pesticides and prevented exports through normal channels to neighbouring states.
"The problem is not the market because traders are ready to buy. The problem is how to take this coffee out of Burundi," Mashwabure said.

OCIBU officials estimate 75 percent of the 1996/97 crop was sold to private buyers abroad and exported by air rather than through by cheaper land and lake routes, reducing profits by at least 30 percent.
"We have lost a lot of money because of the embargo. Air transport is not appropriate for coffee because it is too expensive. It reduced our profits (but) we had no other possibilities," said Minani.
Coffee is Burundi's main foreign exchange earner, bringing in more than 80 percent of its foreign exchange revenues.
Regional sanctions against Burundi were eased in April, boosting traffic with Zambia via Lake Tanganyika.
But Tanzania and its port of Dar es Salaam remained closed.
"(Exporting coffee) through Zambia is four times more expensive than Dar es Salaam," said Charles Ntezahorigwa, managing director of one of Burundi's leading coffee exporters.
